```{.camdl-run show="figure" figure="ppc-r0.svg" caption="An SIR model fitted to a 1978 boarding-school influenza outbreak, re-run on every site build. [Fitting the boarding-school outbreak](guide/first-fit.qmd) walks through it."}
camdl fit run fit-r0.toml --label r0 --seed 4
camdl fit predict @r0
uv run plot_predictive.py ppc-r0.svg SIR=results/fits/fit_r0-*/predict/*/
```

camdl is a modeling language and toolkit for stochastic and deterministic
compartmental models of epidemics. The modeler writes the model as it would
appear on paper (the compartments, the transitions between them and their
rates, the parameters and their priors, and how the data were observed) in one
`.camdl` file. camdl's runtime then simulates it, fits it to data with
particle-based Bayesian methods, and compares it with alternative models. The
modeler writes no simulation or inference code, which is finicky and easy to
get subtly wrong; that code lives once, in camdl's tested runtime.

<!-- figure: architecture, caption: How camdl splits responsibility between the modeler and camdl's developers. The modeler states the model's structure and prior assumptions, and writes no simulation or inference code; camdl's job is to execute the declared model exactly. A trajectory that contradicts the declared model is therefore a bug in camdl, not in the modeler's work, and implementation risk moves from many privately maintained code bases to one shared, tested one. -->

Some of camdl's features:

- **The model is checked by a compiler before it runs.** The compiler checks
  the units and dimensions of every rate, so a per-capita rate used where a
  population rate belongs is a compile error rather than a quietly wrong
  epidemic. While an AI agent built models of the 2026 Bundibugyo ebolavirus
  outbreak, the compiler rejected its models 81 times, a third of them for
  science errors that would otherwise have run and produced a number.
- **Stratification is declared, not hand-written.** Age groups, places and
  disease stages are dimensions, and the compiler expands every compartment and
  transition across them.
- **One model file, several simulators.** The same file runs as an exact
  stochastic simulation (Gillespie), a discrete-time chain-binomial process, or
  a deterministic ODE.
- **Fitting is built in.** Particle Gibbs with Ancestral Sampling (PGAS),
  Particle Marginal Metropolis–Hastings (PMMH) and iterated filtering (IF2) fit
  the stochastic model itself, using gradients the compiler derives from the
  model.
- **A fit reports when it has not converged.** Every fit comes with convergence
  checks and diagnostics, and one that fails them says so instead of printing
  estimates as if it had passed.
- **Runs are reproducible.** Each run is stored under a hash of its model,
  data, settings and camdl version, so the same inputs give the same result,
  and re-running them reads the stored result instead of recomputing it.

## About these docs

Most of these pages also ship inside camdl itself: `camdl docs <topic>` prints
them in your terminal, offline, for the version you have installed. The
tutorials are on the website only, because they show the real output of every
command, re-run against the current code each time the site is built.

Much of this documentation was drafted with a large language model (LLM) and is
being revised by hand. In the tutorials, every command was run when the site
was built, and the output shown is what camdl printed. The guides, concepts and
reference pages are prose checked against the code, and can be wrong. If
something is unclear, contradicts what camdl does, or looks wrong, please
[open an issue](https://github.com/vsbuffalo/camdl/issues/new).
